newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Clinton's peace envoy says Hebron gaps bridgeable.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's peace envoy says Hebron gaps bridgeable.

text.p: Israeli and PLO negotiators, still unable to seal an accord on a troop pullout from Hebron, are to meet on Tuesday despite the absence of President Bill Clinton's peace envoy, officials said.

American envoy Dennis Ross, ending three weeks of marathon mediation in a bid to nail down details of the long-delayed pullout from the West Bank town, said late on Monday the gaps between the sides were "very definitely bridgeable."
Palestinian and Israeli officials said they would meet in Jerusalem on Tuesday to hash out remaining sticking points.
But Israelis were pessimistic on chances of any progress before the return from Europe later this week of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who left for Norway on Monday.

Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh, saying the sides had been only "a number of hours" away from agreement, said he had "not heard of any serious explanation why this trip to Europe was more important than the need to reach agreement on Hebron."
Arafat, in Oslo on the first leg of a three-day tour, said it was Israel that was keeping the deal from being struck.
"I am sorry to say that still the Israelis are making new conditions every day," Arafat said. He said agreement could still be reached on Hebron before U.S. elections on November 5.
Clinton dispatched Ross to the region in the wake of unprecedented Palestinian-Israeli gun battles last month that left scores dead in the West Bank and Gaza.
The mission has since ridden a diplomatic roller-coaster of near-agreements and sudden crises. "I think that agreement is possible," Ross said. "We still have work to do to get it."
Ross packed his bags to leave a week ago, only to be summoned back at the last minute as new hope glimmered for agreement on the long-promised withdrawal from Hebron.
Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns the Jewish state agreed to hand over to Palestinian self-rule.
Israel's previous Labour government agreed to a pullout from the violence-plagued town more than a year ago, but suspended the measure in response to a wave of Islamic suicide bombings.
Palestinians accuse Israel of trying to dictate new terms for the Hebron redeployment, delayed since March. PLO officials say they will brook no alterations to the original agreement.
Israel has said changes are needed to safeguard the 400 Jews who live under heavy army guard in the town of 100,000 Arabs.
The differences centred on Israel's demand for the right to pursue militants into parts of Hebron it hands over, and what arms PLO police would be allowed to carry, Palestinians said.
Hebron, cradle and rallying point of Jewish and Islamic militancy, has caught Netanyahu in the jaws of a political vice.

He is under fierce pressure from his main ally Washington and from the Arab world to order the pullout. But he owes weighty political debts to anti-withdrawal settlers, backed by the National Religious Party (NRP), a key coalition partner.
NRP lawmaker Shaul Yahalom said the party will oppose the accord unless it grants Israel control of "all strategic areas" in Hebron, and bars rifles from PLO police near Jewish homes.
